title: Science Behind the Forecast: The cloud that can look like a UFO
byline: Louisville Public Media | By Bill Burton
excerpt: Every week WAVE 3 meteorologist Tawana Andrew breaks down what we know and what we don't about the climate and weather here in Louisville.
content:
Published November 6, 2026 at 2:02 PM EST

This week on Science Behind the Forecast, we’ll learn about a cloud that can look like a UFO. LPM’s Bill Burton talks about that cloud with meteorologist Tawana Andrew.

This transcript was edited for clarity and length.

Tawana Andrew: Today's topic continues with clouds, but we're focusing on Mother Nature's UFOs.

Bill Burton: The cloud that looks like a UFO. It's called a lenticular cloud. What do we need to know about it?

TA: The reason that we have lenticular clouds is all because of the wind and how it interacts with the Earth's surface. As it blows across the Earth's surface, it interacts with various objects like mountains, hills, even buildings, and that interaction disrupts the wind's flow, creating eddies and making the wind more turbulent downstream.

When you have a stable atmosphere, this turbulence creates what's called a gravity wave downwind from the obstruction. If you have within that gravity wave the air temperature at the crest of the wave dropping to the dew point, then you have condensation happening and those clouds begin to form. But with a stable atmosphere, it resists vertical motion. It wants to be back where it's supposed to be, so the air will return to its original altitude. As that happens, any liquid water will go back to water vapor, and that means you'll see the end of the cloud dissipating. These clouds are continuously developing and dissipating at the crest and the trough of each of these gravity waves, so they look stationary as the wind is flowing quickly through an area.

BB: That's wild. So they're constantly changing, yet they always look the same?

TA: Exactly, which I feel like adds to their spookiness, their mysteriousness.

There are three types of lenticular clouds. There are alto cumulus standing lenticular clouds, stratocumulus lenticular clouds and cirro cumulus lenticular clouds.

BB: Wow, that's a mouthful. What are the differences between the three?

TA: The difference has to do with altitude and the phase of water inside of them. Starting off with the high altitude zero cumulus standing lenticular cloud, because we’ve got to have a long name for everything, right?

BB: Of course, I'd have it no other way.

TA: These are mainly composed of ice crystals, which give them a more delicate, wispy appearance, and these will form well above 18,000 feet. For the alto cumulus lenticular clouds, those are a mixture of ice and water, and they'll form between 8,500 and 24,000 feet, depending on where in the world they are happening. But these are the ones that are really dynamic in how they look, and the ones that are more likely to look like a UFO, they're pretty fluffy. They're very well defined with that lens-like outline, and they're so cool to see in person. They're definitely on my bucket list for sure.

The last one is the stratocumulus lenticular cloud, and that one is made almost entirely of liquid water droplets, it's a lot more rare. You don't get those very often, especially since they form below 8,500 feet. They're a little bit thicker. They're more uniform in appearance, but we just don't see them often.

Lenticular clouds, they're really cool to see, but they're also a very excellent indicator of the turbulence and the waves that are going on in our atmosphere, whether or not we see it or not.
